Appendix B
Appendix to Section
3

B.1
A few properties of Boolean hyperdoctrines

In this section we recall some useful properties of boolean hyperdoctrines, and we prove a lemma which will be crucial for establishing the precise connection with peircean bicategories. All the results we are going to show here are quite natural from the perspective of first-order classical logic, and their proofs are straightforward.

First, it is well-known in first-order classical logic that the universal quantifier can be defined combining the existential quantifier with the negation. In the following lemma we provide a proof using the language of f.o. boolean hyperdoctrine of this fact.

Lemma 49
.

Let
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{Bool}
be a boolean hyperdoctrine. Then for every arrow
f\colon A\to B
, the functor

\forall_{f}(-):=\neg\exists_{f}\neg(-)

provides a right adjoint to
P_{f}
. Moreover, if
\exists_{f}
satisfies BCC then also
\forall_{f}
satisfies BCC.

Proof.

The proof is a straightforward generalization of the ordinary proof in first-order classical logic. Indeed:

\alpha\leq\forall_{f}P_{f}(\alpha)=\neg\exists_{f}\neg P_{f}(\alpha)

holds if and only if

\exists_{f}\neg P_{f}(\alpha)\leq\neg\alpha

because
P
is boolean. But this holds because it is equivalent to

\ P_{f}(\neg\alpha)\leq P_{f}(\neg\alpha).

To prove that

P_{f}\forall_{f}(\beta)\leq\beta

we have to use again the assumption that
P
is boolean. In fact we have that

P_{f}\forall_{f}(\beta)=\neg P_{f}\exists_{f}(\neg\beta)\leq\neg\neg\beta

because
\neg\beta\leq P_{f}\exists_{f}(\neg\beta)
(since
\exists_{f}\dashv P_{f}
), and using the fact that
\neg\neg\beta=\beta
we can conclude that
P_{f}\forall_{f}(\beta)\leq\beta
.
Now we prove that if
\exists_{f}
satisfies BCC then also
\forall_{f}
satisfies BCC. So let us consider a pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

and suppose that
P_{g}\exists_{f}(\alpha)=\exists_{f^{\prime}}P_{g^{\prime}}(\alpha)
for every
\alpha
in
P(A)
. From this we can deduce that
\neg P_{g}\exists_{f}(\alpha)=P_{g}\neg\exists_{f}(\alpha)=\neg\exists_{f^{\prime}}P_{g^{\prime}}(\alpha)
, and then that
P_{g}\forall_{f}(\neg\alpha)=\forall_{f^{\prime}}P_{g^{\prime}}(\neg\alpha)
for every
\alpha
element of
P(A)
. Therefore, in particular it holds for the element
\beta:=\neg\alpha
, and hence (using the fact that
P
is boolean) we can conclude that

P_{g}\forall_{f}(\alpha)=\forall_{f^{\prime}}P_{g^{\prime}}(\alpha)
.
∎

Remark 50

(Frobenius reciprocity)
.

Employing the preservation of the implication
\to
by the functor
P_{f}
, it is straightforward to check that every first-order boolean hyperdoctrine
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{Bool}
satisfies the so-called
Frobenius reciprocity
(FR), namely:

\exists_{f}(P_{f}(\alpha)\wedge\beta)=\alpha\wedge\exists_{f}(\beta)\mbox{ and }\forall_{f}(P_{f}(\alpha)\rightarrow\beta)=\alpha\rightarrow\forall_{f}(\beta)

for every morphism
f\colon X\to Y
,
\alpha
in
P(Y)
and
\beta
in
P(X)
. See
[
34
, Rem. 1.3]
.
However, it is not guarantee that of Beck-Chevalley conditions with respect to pullbacks along
f
. See
[
54
]
for more details.

Lemma 51
.

Let
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{Bool}
be a boolean hyperdoctrine and
\phi\in P(X\times Y)
a functional and entire element from
X
to
Y
. For all
\psi\in P(Y\times Z)
, it holds that

\exists_{\pi_{X\times Z}}(P_{\pi_{X\times Y}}(\phi)\wedge P_{\pi_{Y\times Z}}(\neg\psi))=\neg(\,\exists_{\pi_{X\times Z}}(P_{\pi_{X\times Y}}(\phi)\wedge P_{\pi_{Y\times Z}}(\psi))\,)\text{.}

Proof of
Lemma

24
.

The proof happens to be straightforward if we employ the classical arguments of natural deduction. Here we provide a completely algebric proof.
For sake of readability, here we employ the notation given by the internal language of
P
, writing
\exists y
instead of the left adjoint
\exists_{\pi_{Y}}
and using the predicates
\phi(x,y)
and
\psi(y,z)
to denote the elements
\phi\in P(X\times Y)
and
\psi\in P(Y\times Z)
. Given the well-established correspondence between a doctrine and its internal language, proving that the two previous predicates a equivalent using the logical rules of first-order classical logic is equivalent to prove that they are equal in
P
. Hereafter we thus prove

\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\neg\psi(y,z))=\neg\exists y^{\prime}.(\phi(x,y^{\prime})\wedge\psi(y^{\prime},z))

Therefore, we start by proving

\exists y^{\prime}.(\phi(x,y^{\prime})\wedge\neg\psi(y^{\prime},z))\vdash\neg\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z))

(12)

The crucial point to conclude that (
12
) holds is to show that

\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\vdash\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z).

(13)

holds. In fact, from (
13
) we can deduce the validity of (
12
) because (
13
) implies that

\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z))\vdash\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z)

and hence, by applying to both sides
\neg
, we obtain

\phi(x,y^{\prime})\wedge\neg\psi(y^{\prime},z)\vdash\neg\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z))

and hence that

\exists y^{\prime}.(\phi(x,y^{\prime})\wedge\neg\psi(y^{\prime},z))\vdash\neg\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z))

So we have to prove the validity of (
13
).
Now since we are working with boolean algebras, we have that
\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)=\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\wedge(y=y^{\prime}\vee y\neq y^{\prime})
. Therefore, (
13
) is equivalent to

(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\wedge y=y^{\prime})\vee(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\wedge y\neq y^{\prime})\vdash\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z).

(14)

To prove (
14
), it is enough to prove that both

(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\wedge y=y^{\prime})\vdash\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z)

(15)

and

(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\wedge y\neq y^{\prime})\vdash\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z)

(16)

hold. Now notice that (
16
) holds trivially, because
\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\wedge y=y^{\prime})\vdash\psi(y^{\prime},z)
. To prove (
16
) we have to employ the functionality of
\phi
. In fact, by definition of functionality we have that

\phi(x,y)\wedge\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vdash y=y^{\prime}

and then, using the fact that
y=y^{\prime}
is equivalent to
(y\neq y^{\prime})\to\bot
(were
y\neq y^{\prime}
denotes
\neg(y=y^{\prime})
) we can conclude that

\phi(x,y)\wedge y\neq y^{\prime}\vdash\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})

(17)

and hence that
\phi(x,y)\wedge y\neq y^{\prime}\vdash\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z)
. Therefeore, since
\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)\wedge y\neq y^{\prime}\vdash\phi(x,y)\wedge y\neq y^{\prime}
, we can conclude by transitivity that also (
16
) holds.

This concludes the proof that (
13
), and hence, (
12
) hold.

Now we have to prove that

\neg\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z))\vdash\exists y^{\prime}.(\phi(x,y^{\prime})\wedge\neg\psi(y^{\prime},z))

(18)

First, notice that (
18
) is equivalent to

\forall y^{\prime}.(\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z))\vdash\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z)).

(19)

Now, in order to prove (
19
), we start by employing the assumption that
\phi
is total, namely:

\top\vdash\exists y^{\prime}.\phi(x,y^{\prime}).

(20)

In fact, (
20
) implies that

\forall y^{\prime}.\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vdash\bot

and since in every boolean algebra we have that
\psi(y^{\prime},z)\wedge\neg\psi(y^{\prime},z)\vdash\bot
, we have that

\forall y^{\prime}.\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})=\forall y^{\prime}.(\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\bot)=\forall y^{\prime}.(\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee(\psi(y^{\prime},z)\wedge\neg\psi(y^{\prime},z)))\vdash\bot

(21)

From (
21
), using the distributivity of
\vee
, and the fact that the universal quantifier of a disjunction is equivalent to the disjunction of two universal quantifiers (categorically, right adjoints preserve coproducts), we can conclude that

\forall y^{\prime}.(\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z))\wedge\forall y.(\neg\phi(x,y)\wedge\neg\psi(y,z))\vdash\bot

and hence that

\forall y^{\prime}.(\neg\phi(x,y^{\prime})\vee\psi(y^{\prime},z))\vdash\neg\forall y.(\neg\phi(x,y)\wedge\neg\psi(y,z)).

Now, since
\neg\forall y.(\neg\phi(x,y)\wedge\neg\psi(y,z))=\exists y.(\phi(x,y)\wedge\psi(y,z))
we can conclude that (
19
), and then (
18
) hold.
∎

Appendix C
Appendix to
Section

4

In
Section

4
we have recalled the adjunction between the category of cartesian bicategories
\mathbb{CB}
and that of elementary and existential doctrines
\mathbb{EED}
, i.e.
Equation

7
, from
[
7
]
.
The interested reader may find all details in Sections 5, 6 and 7 of
[
7
]
however, for its convenience, we recall in this appendix some interesting facts that are omitted in the main text.

We start by recalling some details about the
\mathsf{Rel}(-)
construction. The objects, arrows and composition of the category
\mathsf{Rel}(P)
associated to an elementary and existential doctrine
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
are described in
Section

4
. To see why this is a cartesian bicategory it is convenient to first illustrate the monoidal product. For
\phi\colon X\to Y
and
\psi\colon U\to V
arrows of
\mathsf{Rel}(P)
, namely
\phi\in P(X\times Y)
and
\psi\in P(U\times V)
, the arrow
\phi\mathrel{\otimes}\psi\colon X\mathrel{\otimes}U\to Y\mathrel{\otimes}V
is defined as

\phi\mathrel{\otimes}\psi\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}P_{\langle\pi_{X},\pi_{Y}\rangle}(\phi)\wedge P_{\langle\pi_{U},\pi_{V}\rangle}(\psi)

where
\langle\pi_{X},\pi_{Y}\rangle
and
\langle\pi_{U},\pi_{V}\rangle
are the projections from
X\times U\times Y\times Z
to, respectively,
X\times Y
and
U\times V
.

The rest of the structure of cartesian bicategory is inherited from the finite products base category
\mathbf{C}
of
P
by means of the
graph functor

\Gamma_{P}\colon\mathbf{C}\to\mathsf{Rel}(P)
. In particular, the graph functor acts as the identity on objects and mapping each arrow
f\colon X\to Y
in

\Gamma_{P}(f)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}P_{f\times id_{Y}}(\delta_{Y})\in P(X\times Y)=\mathsf{Rel}(P)[X,Y]\text{.}

For instance, for the doctrine
\mathcal{P}\colon\mathsf{Set}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
from
Example

15
, the functor
\Gamma_{\mathcal{P}}\colon\mathsf{Set}\to\mathbf{Rel}^{\circ}
maps every function
f
to its graph.

At this point, it is worth to observe that the arrow
P_{id_{Y}\times f}(\delta_{Y})
is right adjoint to
\Gamma_{P}(f)
(see
[
7
, Pro. 23]
) and thus
\Gamma_{P}(f)
is a map. Therefore,
\Gamma_{P}
restricts to a finite-product preserving functor
\mathbf{C}\to\mathsf{Map}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))
. One can thus define the (co)monoid structure of
\mathsf{Rel}(P)
as

\begin{array}[]{lcrlcr}\blacktriangleleft^{\circ}_{X}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}&\Gamma_{P}(\blacktriangleleft^{\circ}_{X})&\qquad\blacktriangleright^{\circ}_{X}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}&P_{id_{X\times X}\times\blacktriangleleft^{\circ}_{X}}(\delta_{X\times X})\\
{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}&\Gamma_{P}({\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X})&\qquad{\mathclose{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}}}^{\circ}_{X}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}&P_{id_{I}\times{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X}}(\delta_{I})\\
\end{array}

where on the right hand side of the above equation
\blacktriangleleft^{\circ}_{X}\colon X\to X\times X
and
{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X}\colon X\to I
are copier and discard of
\mathbf{C}
(they exist since
\mathbf{C}
has finite products).

The graph functor
\Gamma_{P}\colon\mathbf{C}\to\mathsf{Map}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))
is also used for defining the unit of the adjunction (
7
).
For every elementary and existential doctrine
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
, the morphism of elementary and existential doctrines
\eta_{P}\colon P\to\mathsf{HmI}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))
is

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{InfSl}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathsf{Map}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))^{\operatorname{op}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathsf{Rel}(P)[-,1]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces P}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Gamma_{P}}^{\operatorname{op}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}

(22)

where

•

\Gamma_{P}\colon\mathbf{C}\to\mathsf{Map}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))
is the graph-functor;

•

each component
\rho_{X}\colon P(X)\to\mathsf{Rel}(P)[X,I]\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}P(X\times I)
is given by the isomorphism
P(X)\cong P(X\times I)
obtained by applying the functor
P
to the right unitor
X\times I\cong X
in
\mathbf{C}
.

Proof.

\displaystyle c\vee d

\displaystyle=\neg{(\neg{c}\wedge\neg{d})}

(De Morgan)

\displaystyle=\neg{(\blacktriangleleft^{\circ}_{X}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}(\neg{c}\mathrel{\otimes}\neg{d})\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}\blacktriangleright^{\circ}_{Y})}

(
5
)

\displaystyle=\neg{(\neg{\blacktriangleleft^{\bullet}_{X}}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}\neg{(c\mathrel{\mathbin{\vphantom{\times}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\medbullet$\cr$\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\medbullet$\cr$\textstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptscriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}}}d)}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}\neg{\blacktriangleright^{\bullet}_{Y}})}

(
9
)

\displaystyle=\blacktriangleleft^{\bullet}_{X}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}(c\mathrel{\mathbin{\vphantom{\times}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\medbullet$\cr$\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\medbullet$\cr$\textstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptscriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}}}d)\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}\blacktriangleright^{\bullet}_{Y}

(
9
)

\displaystyle\bot

\displaystyle=\neg{\top}

(De Morgan)

\displaystyle=\neg{({\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathclose{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}}}^{\circ}_{Y})}

(
5
)

\displaystyle=\neg{(\neg{{\mathexclamationmark}^{\bullet}_{X}}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}\neg{{\mathclose{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}}}^{\bullet}_{Y}})}

(
9
)

\displaystyle={\mathexclamationmark}^{\bullet}_{X}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathclose{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}}}^{\bullet}_{Y}

(
9
)

∎

(39)

With this definition at hand it is immediate to show that
\neg{({c}^{\dagger})}=(\neg{c})^{\ddagger}
. Moreover, we show that the two isomorphisms
{(\cdot)}^{\dagger}
and
(\cdot)^{\ddagger}
actually coincide (
Lemma

57
).

Proposition 53
.

For any
c,d\colon X\to Y
the following are equivalent:

1.

c\leq d\qquad

2.

\neg{d}\leq\neg{c}\qquad

3.

\top\leq\neg{c}\vee d\qquad

4.

c\wedge\neg{d}\leq\bot\qquad

Proof.

The four inclusions are equivalent since
\mathbf{C}[X,Y]
is a Boolean algebra.
∎

Lemma 55
.

The following equality holds,
{(\bot_{X,Y})}^{\dagger}=\bot_{Y,X}

Lemma 56
.

For any
c\colon X\to Y
,
{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}=\neg{({c}^{\dagger})}
.

Proof.

We prove the two inclusions separately.
We prove
\leq
, on the left, by means of
Proposition

53
.4. For
\geq
, on the right, we use the properties of
{(\cdot)}^{\dagger}
in
Table

1
and the inclusion proved on the left.

\displaystyle{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}\wedge\neg{\neg{({c}^{\dagger})}}

\displaystyle={(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}\wedge{c}^{\dagger}

(
Definition

25
.1)

\displaystyle={(\neg{c}\wedge c)}^{\dagger}

(
Table

1
)

\displaystyle={(\bot_{X,Y})}^{\dagger}

(
Definition

25
.1)

\displaystyle=\bot_{Y,X}

(
Lemma

55
)

\displaystyle\neg{({c}^{\dagger})}

\displaystyle={{\neg{({c}^{\dagger})}}^{\dagger}}^{\dagger}

(
Table

1
)

\displaystyle\leq{\neg{{{c}^{\dagger}}^{\dagger}}}^{\dagger}

(
{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}\leq\neg{({c}^{\dagger})}
)

\displaystyle={(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}

(
Table

1
)

∎

\displaystyle{c}^{\dagger}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{def:peircean-bicategory}.1}}}{{=}}\;{\left(\neg{\neg{c}}\right)}^{\dagger}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{lemma:dagger preserves negation}}}}{{=}}\;\neg{\left({(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}\right)}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{eqddagger}}}{{=}}\;\left(\neg{\neg{c}}\right)^{\ddagger}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{def:peircean-bicategory}.1}}}{{=}}\;c^{\ddagger}

∎

57
is instrumental in proving the following result that extends (

¬
M

) to
comaps
, i.e. all those arrows
f
, such that
f^{\dagger}
is a map.

Lemma 58
.

For all maps
f\colon X\to Y
and arrows
c\colon Z\to Y
,
\neg{c}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{f}^{\dagger}=\neg{(c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{f}^{\dagger})}

The structure in (
9
) can also be used to define a compact closed structure in
(\mathbf{C},\blacktriangleleft^{\bullet},\blacktriangleright^{\bullet})
. In other words, in a peircean bicategory one can
bend
the wires in two ways. These bending operations are shown to be the same (
Lemma

61
).

∎

Now we need to prove that the axioms of fo-bicategories hold in a peircean bicategory. We do not show a proof for all of them, but only for a few representative ones. The rest are either derivable or proved in a similar manner.

Proposition 62
.

For any
c,d,e\colon X\to Y
,
c\wedge(d\vee e)\leq(c\wedge d)\vee e
.

Proof.

\displaystyle c\wedge(d\vee e)

\displaystyle=(c\wedge d)\vee(c\wedge e)

(Definition
25
.1)

\displaystyle\leq(c\wedge d)\vee(\top\wedge e)

(
Proposition

3
)

\displaystyle=(c\wedge d)\vee e

(Definition
25
.1)

∎

Lemma 65

(Linear distributivities)
.

For any
c\colon X\to Y,d\colon Y\to Z,e\colon Z\to W
, the following inequalities hold

1.

c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}(d\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}e)\leq(c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}d)\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}e\qquad

2.

(c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}d)\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}e\leq c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}(d\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}e)

Proof.

We prove
1.
below by means of
Lemma

45
. The proof for
2.
is analogous.

Lemma 67

(Linear adjoints)
.

For any
c\colon X\to Y
, the following inequalities hold

1.

c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}\leq id^{\bullet}_{X}\qquad

2.

id^{\circ}_{Y}\leq{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}c\qquad

3.

{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}c\leq id^{\bullet}_{Y}\qquad

4.

id^{\circ}_{X}\leq c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}

Proof.

We prove
1.
below.
2.
is proved similarly, exploiting
Proposition

66
.2. The proofs for
3.
and
4.
are analogous.

\begin{array}[]{c@{}c@{}c@{}c@{}c@{}c@{}c}c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{(\neg{c})}^{\dagger}&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\eqref{eqdagger}}}{{=}}&\hbox to66.81pt{\vbox to39.03pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 29.13847pt\lower-17.57138pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \hbox to0.0pt{
{
{}{}{}}{}{{}}{}{
{}{}{}}
{}{}{
{}{}{}}
{}{}{
{}{}{}}

58
)

\displaystyle=\bot_{X\mathrel{\otimes}Z,Y\mathrel{\otimes}W}

(
Lemma

52
)

∎

Proposition 69
.

For any
c,d\colon X\to Y
,
c\wedge d\leq c\vee d
.

Proof.

The following holds since
\mathbf{C}[X,Y]
is a Boolean algebra and a
\wedge
-semilattice with
\top
:

\displaystyle c\wedge d

\displaystyle=c\wedge(d\vee d)

(Idempotency of
\vee
)

Corollary 71

(Linear strenghts II)
.

For all objects
X,Y
, the following inequalities hold

id^{\bullet}_{X}\mathrel{\otimes}id^{\bullet}_{Y}\leq id^{\bullet}_{X}\mathrel{\mathbin{\vphantom{\times}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\medbullet$\cr$\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\medbullet$\cr$\textstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptscriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}}}id^{\bullet}_{Y}\qquad\quad id^{\circ}_{X}\mathrel{\otimes}id^{\circ}_{Y}\leq id^{\circ}_{X}\mathrel{\mathbin{\vphantom{\times}\mathchoice{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\displaystyle\medbullet$\cr$\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\textstyle\medbullet$\cr$\textstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}{\vtop{\halign{#\cr$\scriptscriptstyle\medbullet$\cr$\scriptscriptstyle{\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\times}$\cr}}}}}id^{\circ}_{Y}

Proof.

Immediate by
Lemma

70
.
∎

Proof of
Theorem

26
.

By Propositions
7
and
9
every fo-bicategory is a peircean bicategory. By Proposition
8
every morphism of fo-bicategories is a morphism of peircean bicategories.

Now observe that a peircean bicategory
\mathbf{C}
is a fo-bicategory, since:

•

it is a cartesian bicategory by definition;

•

it is a cocartesian bicategory via the isomorphism
\neg{}\colon(\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{co}},\blacktriangleleft^{\circ},\blacktriangleright^{\circ})\to(\mathbf{C},\blacktriangleleft^{\bullet},\blacktriangleright^{\bullet})
;

•

it is a closed linear bicategory, since:

(

) hold by

;

), (

and (

;

–

every arrow

, and in particular also
\sigma^{\circ},\sigma^{\bullet},\blacktriangleleft^{\circ},{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ},\blacktriangleright^{\circ},{\mathclose{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}}}^{\circ},\blacktriangleleft^{\bullet},{\mathexclamationmark}^{\bullet},\blacktriangleright^{\bullet}
and
{\mathclose{\mathchoice{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\displaystyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\textstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}{\raisebox{0.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathinvertedexclamationmark$}}}}^{\bullet}

A morphism of peircean bicategories

preserves the structure defined in (

) since it preserves negation, e.g.

\displaystyle F(c\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}d)

\displaystyle=F(\neg{(\neg{c}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}\neg{d})})

c

c

is both functional and entire if and only if

Y

Proof of
Proposition

29
.

By
Equation

7
we have that for every elementary and existential doctrine
P
, the unit of the adjunction
\mathsf{Rel}(-)\dashv\mathsf{HmI}(-)
is morphism of elementary and existential doctrines
\eta_{P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{\tiny def}}}{{=}}(\Gamma_{P},\rho)\colon P\to\mathsf{HmI}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))
. Moreover, each component of
\rho
is an iso by definition (see
Appendix

C
for a detailed description). Therefore,
\rho
preserves and reflects functional and entire relations (see
Remark

18
), i.e.
\rho_{X\times Y}(\phi)\in\mathsf{Rel}(P)[X\times Y,I]
is functional and entire in
\mathsf{Rel}(P)
if and only if
\phi
is functional and entire in
P
. On the other hand, by
Lemma

74
we have that an arrow
\psi\in\mathsf{Rel}(P)[X,Y]
, i.e. an element
\psi\in P(X\times Y)
, is a map if and only if the corresponding element in
\mathsf{Rel}(P)[A\times B,I]
, i.e.
\rho_{X\times Y}(\psi)
, is functional and entire with respect to the doctrine
\mathsf{Rel}(P)[-,I]
. Therefore, we can conclude that
\phi
is a map in
\mathsf{Rel}(P)
if and only if
\phi
is an entire and functional element of
P
.
∎

Proof of
Theorem

31
.

First, we want to prove that the inclusion
\mathsf{HmI}\colon\mathbb{CB}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{EED}
in (
7
) restricts to an inclusion of categories

\mathbb{PB}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{BHD}
. By
Proposition

27
, one only needs to check for morphisms in
\mathbb{PB}
. Given a morphism of peircean bicategories
F\colon\mathbf{C}\to\mathbf{D}
,
\mathsf{HmI}(F)
is the morphism of elementary and existential doctrines
(\tilde{F},\mathfrak{b}^{F})
defined in
Section

4
. In order to conclude that it is a morphism of boolean doctrines, it is enough to show that
\mathfrak{b}^{F}_{X}
is a morphism of boolean algebras for all objects
X
. Since
(\tilde{F},\mathfrak{b}^{F})
is a morphism of doctrines,
\mathfrak{b}^{F}_{X}
is a morphism of inf-semilattices. Thus it is enough to show that
\mathfrak{b}^{F}_{X}
preserve negation. But this is trivial since, for all
c\in\mathbf{C}[X,I]
,

\displaystyle\mathfrak{b}^{F}_{X}(\neg{c})

\displaystyle=F(\neg{c})

(Def.
\mathfrak{b}^{F}
)

\displaystyle=\neg{F(c)}

(morphism of Peircean,
Definition

25
)

\displaystyle=\neg{\mathfrak{b}^{F}_{X}(c)}

(Def.
\mathfrak{b}^{F}
)

Now, to prove that
\mathsf{Rel}
restrict to a functor
\mathsf{Rel}\colon\mathbb{BHD}\to\mathbb{PB}
, by
Proposition

30
, one only needs to check that for all morphisms of boolean hyperdoctrines
(F,\mathfrak{b})\colon P\to Q
,
\mathsf{Rel}(F,\mathfrak{b})\colon\mathsf{Rel}(P)\to\mathsf{Rel}(Q)
is a morphism of peicean bicategories. Since by (
7
),
\mathsf{Rel}(F,\mathfrak{b})
is a morphism of cartesian bicategories, one only needs to check that it preserves the negation. But this is obvious since for all arrows
\phi\in\mathsf{Rel}(P)[X,Y]
,
\mathsf{Rel}(F,\mathfrak{b})(\phi)
is –by definition–
\mathfrak{b}_{X\times Y}(\phi)
and
\mathfrak{b}_{X\times Y}
is a morphism of boolean algebras.

To conclude, one only needs to check the unit and the counit of the adjunction in (
7
). The counit is an isomorphism of cartesian bicategories (see Equation (9) in
[
7
]
), and then it provides an isomorphism of peircean bicategories
\mathbf{C}\cong\mathsf{Rel}(\mathbf{C}[-,I])
whenever
\mathbf{C}
is a peircean bicategory.
The unit of the adjunction
\eta_{P}\colon P\to\mathsf{Rel}(P)[-,I]
is the morphism of elementary and existential doctrines
(\Gamma_{P},\rho)
illustrated in (
22
). To conclude that
\eta_{P}
is a morphism of boolean hyperdoctrine whenever
P
is a boolean hyperdoctrine, one has only to prove that
\rho
is a morphism of boolean algebras, but this is trivial since
\rho
is always an isomorphism of inf-semilattices.

∎

Appendix F
Appendix to
Section

7

Proof of
Theorem

36
.

By
Equation

8
we have that the
\mathsf{HmI}
and
\mathsf{Rel}
functors provide an equivalence between the categories
\mathbb{CB}
and
\overline{\mathbb{EED}}
. Now, since every peircean category is in particular a cartesian bicategory, we have that every boolean hyperdoctrine arising from a peircean bicategory satisfies (RUC) and it has comprehensive diagonals. Then, we have that the functor
\mathsf{HmI}\colon\mathbb{PB}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{BHD}
factors through the canonical inclusion
\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{BHD}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{PB}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{BHD}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{HmI}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathsf{HmI}}

By
Theorem

31
, we have that
\mathsf{HmI}\colon\mathbb{PB}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{BHD}
is fully and faithful (since the counit of the adjunction is an iso), so it remains to prove that it is essentially surjective (with respect to the objects of
\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}
). By the equivalence presented in
Equation

8
, we know that every boolean hyperdoctrine (that is in particular an elementary and existential doctrine) satisfying (RUC) and having comprehensive diagonals, is isomorphic to an elementary and existential doctrine
\mathbf{C}[-,I]\colon\mathsf{Map}(\mathbf{C})^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
for some cartesian bicategory
\mathbf{C}
. Thus, we can conclude that
\mathbf{C}[-,I]\colon\mathsf{Map}(\mathbf{C})^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
is a boolean hyperdoctrine and, by
Corollary

28
, that
\mathbf{C}
is a peircean bicategory. This concludes the proof that
\mathbb{PB}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}
.

∎

Appendix G
Appendix to
Section

8

We summarize some useful properties of tabulations, which are crucial to establish the precise connection with the notion of full comprehension. We refer to
[
12
, Lem. 3.3]
for the following result:

Lemma 75
.

Let
i\colon X_{r}\to X
be a tabulation of
r\colon X\to I
. Then

•

for every map
f\colon Z\to X
such that
f^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{Z}\leq r
there exists a unique map
h\colon Z\to X_{r}
such that
f=h\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}i
;

•

if
f^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{Z}=r
, then
h^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{Z}={\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X}
.

Now we recall another useful lemma, regarding doctrines with full comprehensions. We refer to
[
54
, Pro. 7.10]
for the following result:

Lemma 76
.

Let
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
be a doctrine with full comprehensions. Then
every comprehension is a mono for every element
\alpha
of
P(X)
we have that
\alpha=\exists_{\{\alpha\}}(\top_{X_{\alpha}})
.

Proof of
Theorem

41
.

Let
(\mathbf{C},\blacktriangleleft^{\circ},\blacktriangleright^{\circ})
be functionally complete, and let us consider the doctrine
\mathbf{C}[-,I]\colon\mathsf{Map}(\mathbf{C})^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
and an element
r\colon X\to I
of
\mathbf{C}[X,I]
. We claim that the tabulation
i\colon X_{r}\to X
of
r
is the comprehension of
r
.

First, notice that
\mathbf{C}[i,I](r)=\top_{X_{r}}
(i.e.
i\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}r={\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r}}
) because, by definition of functionally completeness, we have that
i\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}i^{\dagger}=\operatorname{id}_{X_{r}}
and
i^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r}}=r
, and hence
i\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}r={\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r}}
. Now suppose that
f\colon Z\to X
is a map such that
\mathbf{C}[f,I](r)=\top_{Z}
(i.e.
f\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}r={\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{Z}
). Then, in particular, we have that
\top_{Z}\leq\mathbf{C}[f,I](r)
, and we can conclude that
\exists_{f}(\top_{X_{r}})\leq r
because the doctrine
\mathbf{C}[-,I]\colon\mathsf{Map}(\mathbf{C})^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
is elementary and existential, so it has left adjoints along all the arrows (see
Remark

13
). Now, by definition of left ajoints for this doctrine (see
Example

16
) this means that
f^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{Z}\leq r
, so we can apply
Lemma

75
and conclude that there exists a unique
h
such that
f=h\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}i
. This concludes the proof that if
(\mathbf{C},\blacktriangleleft^{\circ},\blacktriangleright^{\circ})
is functionally complete then
\mathbf{C}[-,I]\colon\mathsf{Map}(\mathbf{C})^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
has comprehensions.

Now we need to prove that comprehensions are full. So let
r,r^{\prime}\colon X\to I
be two arrows and let
i
and
i^{\prime}
their tabulation. If
i
factors through
i^{\prime}
, namely
i=g\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}i^{\prime}
for some map
g\colon X_{r}\to X_{r^{\prime}}
, then we have that
i^{\dagger}=(i^{\prime})^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}g^{\dagger}
. Hence, we can conclude that
r\leq r^{\prime}
because, by hypothesis,
i^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r}}=r
, and using the fact that
i^{\dagger}=(i^{\prime})^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}g^{\dagger}
, we can conclude that
r=(i^{\prime})^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}g^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r}}\leq r^{\prime}
(because
(i^{\prime})^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r^{\prime}}}=r^{\prime}
and
g^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r}}\leq{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r^{\prime}}}
).

Now we show that full comprehensions implies functionally completeness. So, let us consider an arrow
r\colon X\to I
. We claim that the comprehension
\{r\}\colon X_{r}\to X
is a tabulation of
r
. First, by
Lemma

76
, we have that
\exists_{\{r\}}(\top_{X_{r}})=r
, namely that
\{r\}^{\dagger}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}{\mathexclamationmark}^{\circ}_{X_{r}}=r
. Finally, we have that
\{r\}\mathbin{\hbox{\hskip 3.1597pt\hskip-1.38889pt\hbox{$,$}\hskip-1.38889pt\hskip-3.1597pt\raisebox{1.85555pt}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\circ$}}\hskip-3.1597pt\hskip 3.1597pt}}\{r\}^{\dagger}=\operatorname{id}_{X_{r}}
because comprehensions are monomorphisms in
\mathsf{Map}(\mathbf{C})
. This concludes the proof that
\{r\}
is the tabulation of
r
.
∎

The last part of this section is devoted to prove the final corollary, namely that

\mathbb{PB}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}_{c}\cong\mathbb{BC}

To properly reach this goal, we summarize here in the language of doctrines the main results presented in this work, and some useful characterizations presented in
[
50
]
. Our result will follow by combining these results.

First, we have the following result presented in
[
7
, Thm. 35]
:

Theorem 77
.

Let
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
be an elementary and existential doctrine. Then the following two conditions are equivalent:

•

P
has comprehensive diagonals and satisfies (RUC);

•

\mathbf{C}\cong\mathsf{Map}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))
and
P\cong\mathbf{C}[-,I]
.

In particular,
\mathbb{CB}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{EED}}
.

Combining the previous result with
Theorem

41
we obtain the following corollary, where we denote by
\overline{\mathbb{EED}}_{c}
the full subcategory of
\overline{\mathbb{EED}}
given by those doctrines of
\overline{\mathbb{EED}}
having full comprehensions, and by
\mathbb{CB}_{f}
the full subcategory of
\mathbb{CB}
given by functionally complete cartesian bicategories.

Corollary 78
.

Let
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
be an elementary and existential doctrine. Then the following two conditions are equivalent:

•

P
has comprehensive diagonals, full comprehension and satisfies (RUC);

•

\mathbf{C}\cong\mathsf{Map}(\mathsf{Rel}(P))
,
\mathbf{C}
is functionally complete and
P\cong\mathbf{C}[-,I]
.

In particular,
\mathbb{CB}_{f}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{EED}}_{c}
.

Notice that
Theorem

77
can be seen as a generalization of another result regarding doctrines and regular categories presented in
[
50
, Prop. 5.3]
, establishing the precise connection between regular categories and doctrines:

Theorem 79
.

Let
P\colon\mathbf{C}^{\operatorname{op}}\longrightarrow\mathsf{InfSl}
be an elementary and existential doctrine. Then the following two conditions are equivalent:

•

P
has comprehensive diagonals, full comprehensions and satisfies (RUC);

•

\mathbf{C}
is regular and
P\cong\mathsf{Sub}_{\mathbf{C}}
.

In particular,
\mathbb{REG}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{EED}}_{c}
.

Finally, we can combine the previous result with
Corollary

78
obtaining as corollary the well-known equivalence (see
[
12
]
and
[
24
]
) between functionally complete bicategories and regular categories:

Corollary 80
.

We have the equivalences of categories
\mathbb{REG}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{EED}}_{c}\equiv\mathbb{CB}_{f}
.

Since, by definition (see
[
38
, Sec. A1.4, p. 38]
), a category
\mathbf{C}
is boolean if and only if the subobjects functor on
\mathbf{C}
is a boolean hyperdoctrine, we have the following corollary, that is a particular instance of the previous one. Here we denote the category of boolean categories by
\mathbb{BC}
and that of boolean hyperodctrines satisfying (RUC), with full comprehensions and comprehensive diagonals by
\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}_{c}
:

Corollary 81
.

We have an equivalence of categories
\mathbb{BC}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}_{c}
.

Combining these results we obtain the proof of our finial corollary:

Proof of
Corollary

42
.

By
Theorem

36
we have the equivalences
\mathbb{FOB}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}
, so we can combine this result with
Corollary

78
obtaining the equivalence
\mathbb{FOB}_{f}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}_{c}
. Therefore, combining this equivalence with
Corollary

81
we obtain

\mathbb{FOB}_{f}\equiv\overline{\mathbb{BHD}}_{c}\equiv\mathbb{BC}.

∎
